title: Why humans have festivals at all

hero.headline: Why humans have festivals at all: 12,000 years of feasts, fire-walks and the science of the crowd

prequestions.prompt: Archaeology shows people built farms and towns first, and only later began holding big festive gatherings.
prequestions.explanation: Göbekli Tepe's carved pillars and feasting debris date to about 9500 BCE, built by hunter-gatherers before farming took hold. Gathering may have come first.

prequestions.prompt: In a Spanish fire-walking festival, whose heart rhythms rose and fell in step with the fire-walkers?
prequestions.explanation: Friends and relatives in the crowd synchronised with walkers; unrelated spectators did not (Konvalinka et al., 2011).

prequestions.prompt: At Thaipusam in Mauritius, did people who performed or watched the painful kavadi give more or less to the temple than people at a low-pain prayer?
prequestions.explanation: More. Both performers and observers of the high-ordeal ritual donated more, and higher reported pain went with bigger gifts.

prequestions.prompt: Pilgrims who spent a month camping at the freezing, crowded Magh Mela reported worse health afterwards than neighbours who stayed home.
prequestions.explanation: The reverse: their self-reported health improved, and the researchers credited shared identity (Tewari et al., 2012).

prequestions.prompt: Roughly how many bathers did the Uttar Pradesh government claim for the 45-day Maha Kumbh in 2025?
prequestions.explanation: 66.21 crore, about 662 million: a government figure that cannot be independently checked, but even far lower estimates make it the largest gathering ever.

sections.title: A party older than farming
sections.intro_md:
Around **9500 BCE**, on a limestone ridge in what is now south-east Turkey, people who had never planted a field dragged stone pillars up to **5.5 metres** tall into rings and carved them with foxes, boars, snakes and vultures. They had no metal tools, no pack animals and no wheel. The rubbish they left behind is mostly the bones of wild gazelle and aurochs, eaten in bulk.

That site is **Göbekli Tepe**, and it turns the usual story upside down. We tend to think people first settled down, grew food, built towns, and only then found time for celebrations. The stones suggest the order may have been closer to the reverse: the urge to gather, feast and mark something special together came early, and may even have pushed people towards farming.

So today's question is: why does every human society ever studied stop work, spend its savings, dress up, light fires, sing in unison and sometimes hurt itself on a fixed date, year after year? By the end you will have six answers, and your next Diwali or Eid will look different.

spotlights.name: Göbekli Tepe
spotlights.when: From about 9500 BCE; UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2018
spotlights.spot_it: Rings of giant T-shaped limestone pillars, carved with animals, sunk into a hilltop under a modern protective roof.
spotlights.story_md: German archaeologist **Klaus Schmidt** began digging here in **1995** and called it the world's first temple, a place where hunter-gatherers met to feast and build. The T-shaped pillars are thought to be stylised people: some have carved arms and hands meeting over a belt. Excavators found huge numbers of gazelle and aurochs bones and large stone basins that some researchers think held fermented grain, an early beer, though no one has proved it. Since Schmidt's death in 2014, newer work has found houses and water cisterns, so the site was probably also lived in. The feasting part of the story has survived that revision.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It suggests big communal gatherings came before farming and cities, not after.
spotlights.memory_hook: Before the first farm, there was the first party venue.

spotlights.name: The Hilazon Tachtit funeral feast

where.label: Hilazon Tachtit cave, western Galilee, Israel

spotlights.spot_it: A small cave in the hills of the western Galilee, Israel; the evidence is burnt tortoise shells and wild cattle bones in two pits.
spotlights.story_md: About **12,000 years ago**, people of the Natufian culture buried an older woman, probably a healer or shaman, in this cave. Around her body they placed tortoise shells, and in two hollows nearby they left the remains of a feast: at least **71 tortoises** and **three aurochs**, the huge wild cattle of the Ice Age. The tortoises alone would have fed about **35 people**. Natalie Munro and Leore Grosman published it in **2010** as the oldest clear evidence of a planned communal feast. The menu tells you it took effort: tortoises have to be collected one by one, over days.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The oldest securely dated feast we know is a funeral, a gathering to mark a death.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first recorded party was a wake with 71 tortoises on the menu.

sections.title: What counts as a festival, in numbers
sections.intro_md:
A festival is a gathering that a community repeats on purpose, at a set time, where ordinary rules are suspended or flipped for a while. That last part is the key. A market day is a gathering. A festival is a gathering where you are *supposed* to eat too much, stay up all night, dress as someone else, give things away, or throw coloured powder at a stranger.

Festivals sit on a spectrum. At one end are solemn rites such as **Pitru Paksha** or **Yom Kippur**, about duty and memory. At the other are carnivals, built on noise and licence. Most real festivals mix the two: Diwali has both a puja and a firecracker war; Christmas has both a midnight mass and an office party.

The scale today is unlike anything in history. The six numbers on this page are the ones worth carrying around. The biggest gatherings our species has ever organised are festivals, not wars, sports events or political rallies.

spotlights.name: Chunyun, the Spring Festival rush
spotlights.when: 40 days around Chinese New Year; 2026 rush ran 2 February to 13 March
spotlights.spot_it: Railway stations packed wall to wall with travellers carrying gifts and luggage in the weeks before Lunar New Year.
spotlights.story_md: Every year hundreds of millions of Chinese workers go home for the Spring Festival, mostly to reunite with parents and grandparents. Officials count every inter-regional trip, so the numbers are huge: the **2026** rush logged a record **9.41 billion** trips in 40 days, up **4.3%** on 2025. Most were by road (8.74 billion); rail carried about **540 million**. On the single busiest day, 20 February 2026, there were about **353 million** trips. The reason is not religion. It is family: for many migrant workers this is the only week of the year they see their children.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the largest annual human migration, driven by a festival of reunion.
spotlights.memory_hook: Once a year, China moves more than its own population, many times over, just to get home for dinner.

sections.title: Stones, pigs and the shortest day
sections.intro_md:
Archaeologists cannot dig up a song or a mood. They can dig up rubbish, and festival rubbish has a signature: too many animals eaten in one place at one time, cooking pits far larger than one family needs, and buildings aimed at the sky.

The best evidence comes from Neolithic Britain and Ireland, around 3200 to 2500 BCE. Big stone monuments there were lined up on the sunrise or sunset of the **winter solstice**, the shortest day of the year. Animal bones show people travelling hundreds of kilometres to eat together at exactly that time. The pattern repeats across the world: once people can count the year, they mark its turning points, and they mark them with food.

Why the solstice? In a farming or herding year, midwinter is the moment of greatest worry. Stores are falling, the sun is weakest, and nobody can be sure it will come back. A shared feast at the darkest point says: we got this far, together, and the light will return.

spotlights.name: Durrington Walls
spotlights.spot_it: A huge circular bank and ditch, 3 km from Stonehenge, beside a ring of concrete posts (Woodhenge) marking a vanished timber circle.
spotlights.story_md: Excavations here found more than **38,000** animal bones, about **90%** of them from pigs. Analysis of the teeth shows many pigs were killed at about **nine months** old; since piglets are born in spring, that points to slaughter in **midwinter**. Isotopes in the teeth show some pigs were raised as far away as west Wales, northern England and north-east Scotland, so people drove live animals hundreds of kilometres to the feast. Some pigs were roasted, others boiled in pots. The settlement may have held up to **4,000** people at a time. It was probably where the builders of Stonehenge partied.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the clearest evidence of a seasonal mass feast in prehistoric Europe.
spotlights.memory_hook: Stonehenge was the cathedral; Durrington Walls was the barbecue.

spotlights.name: Newgrange
spotlights.spot_it: A large round mound faced with white quartz, with a carved spiral stone at the entrance and a small 'roof box' above the door.
spotlights.story_md: Newgrange in Ireland is older than Stonehenge's stone circle and the Great Pyramid of Giza. For a few mornings around the **winter solstice**, sunlight shines through a slot above the door, called the roof box, and creeps **19 metres** down the passage to light the chamber floor for about **17 minutes**. The rest of the year the chamber is dark. Each year tens of thousands of people enter a lottery for a few dozen places inside on those mornings. If the sky is cloudy, there is nothing to see.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that people engineered buildings around a single shared annual moment.
spotlights.memory_hook: A 5,000-year-old building that switches its own light on once a year.

sections.title: Clocks made of parties
sections.intro_md:
Before printed calendars, festivals *were* the calendar. A farmer did not think "21 December"; she thought "after the midwinter feast", "before the spring new year". Festivals pinned the year to the sky, and they told everyone when to sow, when to reap, when to pay debts and when to marry.

That is why so many festivals sit on the same few dates across unrelated cultures. Winter solstice gave us Saturnalia, Yule, Dongzhi in China and the Inca Inti Raymi (in June, because the southern hemisphere's winter is in June). Spring equinox gave Nowruz, Akitu and many new years. Harvest gave Pongal, Onam, Thanksgiving and the Chinese Mid-Autumn Festival. The moon gave Eid, Diwali, Holi and the Lantern Festival, which is why their dates drift on the solar calendar.

Calendar festivals also do political work: whoever controls the festival controls time.

spotlights.name: Akitu, the Babylonian new year
spotlights.when: Recorded from about 2000 BCE to Roman times
spotlights.spot_it: The blue glazed-brick Ishtar Gate with yellow lions and dragons, through which the procession passed.
spotlights.story_md: For about **12 days** at the spring new year, Babylon carried the statue of its god **Marduk** in procession through the Ishtar Gate along the Processional Way. The strangest moment came on day five: the high priest took away the king's crown and sceptre, made him kneel, and **slapped his face**. If tears came, the god was pleased and the king's reign would be renewed. The ritual reminded everyone, including the king, that power was granted, not owned. The rebuilt Ishtar Gate now stands in the Pergamon Museum, Berlin.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows festivals used to reset the social order every year, including the ruler's place in it.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Babylon, the new year began with a priest slapping the king until he cried.

spotlights.name: Saturnalia
spotlights.spot_it: Romans at a feast in loose clothes and felt freedmen's caps, masters serving slaves at table.
spotlights.story_md: Saturnalia began on **17 December** and stretched to a week. Shops and courts shut, gambling was allowed in public, people swapped the toga for a casual dinner tunic and wore the felt **pileus**, the cap of a freed slave. Masters served their slaves at table, and a mock 'king' was chosen by dice to give silly orders. People gave each other wax candles and small clay figures. The poet **Catullus** called it the best of days. The writer **Pliny the Younger** built a soundproof room in his villa so he could work while his household partied.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Many later winter customs, from gift-giving to a lord of misrule, echo it.
spotlights.memory_hook: For one week a year, Rome let the slaves be served.

spotlights.name: Inti Raymi
spotlights.spot_it: A costumed 'Sapa Inca' and hundreds of performers in red, gold and black on the grass below the zigzag walls of Sacsayhuamán.
spotlights.story_md: The Inca held their greatest festival at the **June solstice**, the southern hemisphere's shortest day, to honour **Inti**, the sun god, and ask him to return. Spanish authorities and the Church suppressed it in the 16th century. In **1944** a group in Cusco led by the writer Faustino Espinoza Navarro revived it as a theatrical pageant in Quechua, staged at the Inca fortress of **Sacsayhuamán**. Today it draws tens of thousands of visitors and is one of South America's biggest festivals. It is a reconstruction, not a continuous tradition, and that is part of its point: a people reclaiming its own calendar.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how festivals can be banned, remembered and rebuilt as identity.
spotlights.memory_hook: The Inca sun party was banned for nearly four centuries and came back in 1944.

spotlights.name: The serpent of Chichén Itzá
spotlights.spot_it: A stepped Maya pyramid in late afternoon, with a zigzag of triangular light and shadow running down the edge of the north staircase to a carved serpent head.
spotlights.story_md: On the afternoons around the **equinoxes**, the stepped corner of El Castillo casts seven triangles of light down its northern stairs, joining the stone serpent head at the bottom. It looks like a snake of light sliding to earth, and it draws huge crowds every March. Was it designed that way? Experts disagree. The effect is visible for weeks around each equinox, not only on the day, and no Maya text describes it. What is certain is that people gather for it now. A festival can grow around a shared moment even when its origin is unknown.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a test case for separating real ancient design from modern festival myth.
spotlights.memory_hook: Whether the Maya meant it or not, the snake gets an audience every March.

sections.title: The electric crowd
sections.intro_md:
The first big theory of why festivals exist came from a French sociologist who never attended the ceremonies he wrote about. In **1912**, **Émile Durkheim** published *The Elementary Forms of Religious Life*, built on reports of Aboriginal Australian gatherings. He noticed that groups who lived scattered for most of the year came together for intense ceremonies of dancing, singing and chanting, and that people described feeling lifted out of themselves.

Durkheim called that feeling **collective effervescence**: the fizzing energy of a crowd that shares one focus. His bold claim was that this is where the sacred comes from. People feel a force bigger than themselves, and that force is real: it is the group. The festival recharges the group's sense of itself, and then everyone goes home to ordinary life until the next one.

For most of the 20th century this was a clever idea with no measurements. In **2011**, a team of researchers wired up a village in Spain and measured it, using heart-rate monitors on people walking over burning coals and on the people watching them.

spotlights.name: Émile Durkheim
spotlights.spot_it: A balding, bearded French academic in a high collar, in old studio portraits.
spotlights.story_md: Durkheim was the son and grandson of rabbis, and he trained to be one before turning to philosophy and then founding sociology as an academic subject in France. He never did fieldwork in Australia. His theory of religion rested on reports by **Baldwin Spencer and Francis Gillen** about the Arrernte (then written Arunta) of central Australia. His key move was to treat the gathering itself, not the gods, as the engine: the feeling of being part of a crowd is so strong that people experience it as something sacred. His only son, André, was killed in the First World War in 1915, and Durkheim died two years later.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He gave us the idea that festivals are how a society feels itself exist.
spotlights.memory_hook: Durkheim's god was the crowd.

spotlights.name: Corroboree
spotlights.spot_it: Aboriginal dancers with white ochre body paint, moving to clapsticks and song, often at night around fires.
spotlights.story_md: A corroboree is an Aboriginal Australian ceremonial gathering of dance, song and story. The English word was borrowed in the early colonial years from the **Dharug** language of the Sydney area. Some corroborees are open, social events; others are sacred and restricted to initiated people. Ceremonies like these, described secondhand by 19th-century ethnographers, became the raw material for Durkheim's theory. Aboriginal communities today stress that these are living traditions with their own owners and rules, not a window onto 'primitive' religion, which is how European theorists once framed them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the real practice behind the most famous theory of festivals, and a reminder to frame it respectfully.
spotlights.memory_hook: The European theory of the sacred crowd began with someone else's dance.

spotlights.name: The fire-walk heart study
spotlights.spot_it: Barefoot men carrying people on their backs across a short carpet of glowing embers in a stone amphitheatre at night.
spotlights.story_md: Every **23 June**, on the night of San Juan, men in the Spanish village of **San Pedro Manrique** (about 600 people) walk barefoot across a bed of glowing coals, often carrying someone on their back, in an amphitheatre that seats up to **3,000**. Researchers led by **Ivana Konvalinka** and **Dimitris Xygalatas** put heart-rate monitors on fire-walkers and spectators. The heart rhythms of walkers and their **friends and relatives in the crowd** rose and fell in step. Unrelated tourists sitting in the same stands did not synchronise. It was the first physical measurement of something like Durkheim's collective effervescence.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows festival feeling is a measurable, shared bodily state, shaped by who you are bonded to.
spotlights.memory_hook: At the fire-walk, families share one heartbeat; strangers do not.

sections.title: Doors in time
sections.intro_md:
In **1909** the Dutch-French folklorist **Arnold van Gennep** noticed that ceremonies for birth, puberty, marriage, death and the new year all share the same three-step shape. First you are **separated** from your old status. Then you pass through a strange in-between period. Then you are **incorporated** back into society in your new role. He called them *rites de passage*.

Fifty years later the British anthropologist **Victor Turner**, working among the Ndembu of Zambia, zoomed in on the middle step. He called it **liminal**, from the Latin for threshold, and described people in it as "betwixt and between": no longer what they were, not yet what they will be. In that state, ordinary ranks fall away and people feel an intense, equal togetherness that Turner called **communitas**.

Many festivals are rites of passage for a whole community. New year is the obvious one: the old year is killed off, there is a night of chaos, and the new year is welcomed in. Pilgrimages work the same way. You leave home, live rough among strangers dressed like you, and return changed. A modern desert arts festival, as you will see, was practically built from Turner's book.

spotlights.name: Arnold van Gennep
spotlights.spot_it: A dark-haired, moustached European scholar in early 20th-century portraits.
spotlights.story_md: Van Gennep was born in Germany to a Dutch father and grew up in France. He published *Les Rites de Passage* in **1909**, but French academia, dominated by Durkheim's school, largely ignored him, and he never held a permanent professorship in France. He spent much of his life cataloguing French folk customs instead, producing a vast multi-volume handbook. His three-stage model, separation, transition and incorporation, only became famous in English after a 1960 translation. Today it is one of the most used ideas in anthropology.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He gave us the shape that almost every ceremony and festival follows.
spotlights.memory_hook: Every festival is a door: step out, wait in the doorway, step back in.

spotlights.name: Burning Man
spotlights.when: Late August to early September; Black Rock Desert since 1990
spotlights.spot_it: A tall wooden human figure on a platform in a flat white desert, surrounded by a temporary city of tents, art cars and dust.
spotlights.story_md: Burning Man began in **1986** when Larry Harvey and Jerry James burned an 8-foot wooden figure on Baker Beach, San Francisco. It moved to Nevada's **Black Rock Desert** in 1990. Now about **70,000 to 80,000** people build a temporary town there each year, live by a 'gift economy' in which almost nothing is for sale, burn the Man and a temple, and then must remove every trace. It is a rite of passage in Turner's sense: separation in a hostile desert, a liminal week in costume, return to 'default world'. The **2026** edition reported three deaths, a reminder that remote mass gatherings carry real risk.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a deliberately designed modern festival built on old ritual logic.
spotlights.memory_hook: A city that exists for nine days and then burns its own idol.

sections.title: The world turned upside down
sections.intro_md:
Some festivals are not about togetherness at all. They are about **disorder**: men dressing as women, servants giving orders, the poor mocking the rich, the church mocking itself. Why would any society schedule its own rebellion?

Two big answers compete. The Russian critic **Mikhail Bakhtin**, writing about medieval carnival, saw it as a genuine second life for ordinary people, a time of laughter, food and bodily freedom that exposed official power as temporary and a bit ridiculous. The British anthropologist **Max Gluckman**, studying rituals in south-east Africa in **1954**, saw something more conservative: "rituals of rebellion" that let people let off steam once a year, so the system survives the other 364 days. A carnival, in that view, is a safety valve.

Both are probably true at different times. Carnival has sometimes turned into real riot and protest, from 16th-century France to 1970s London.

spotlights.name: Mikhail Bakhtin
spotlights.spot_it: An elderly Russian scholar with a lined face, often photographed seated, sometimes with a cigarette.
spotlights.story_md: Bakhtin wrote his book on the French writer Rabelais and medieval carnival around **1940**, as a doctoral thesis, while living in internal exile under Stalin with a leg later amputated because of bone disease. The thesis was argued over for years and the book, *Rabelais and His World*, was not published until **1965**. In it he described **carnival** as a world where everyone takes part, nobody just watches, hierarchy is suspended and the body (eating, drinking, laughing) is celebrated. The word **carnivalesque**, now used for everything from comedy to protest, comes from him.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He gave us the language to see festive disorder as meaningful, not just noise.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bakhtin: in carnival there is no audience, only players.

spotlights.name: The Fight Between Carnival and Lent
spotlights.spot_it: A crowded Flemish town square seen from above; a fat man astride a barrel with a pork spit faces a thin figure on a cart holding a paddle with two herrings.
spotlights.story_md: Pieter Bruegel the Elder painted this square full of more than 150 people. On the left, near an inn, the fat figure of **Carnival** rides a beer barrel, jousting with a spit of roast pork. On the right, near a church, gaunt **Lent** sits on a cart, armed with a baker's paddle holding two fish. Around them people play dice, beg, sell waffles, perform a farce and leave church. It captures the whole carnival idea in one image: a burst of meat and mischief, followed by forty days of fasting before Easter. It hangs in the Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the best single picture of why carnival exists: it is the feast before the fast.
spotlights.memory_hook: Carnival comes from 'carne levare', putting away the meat.

spotlights.name: Rio Carnival
spotlights.when: Five days before Ash Wednesday; Sambadrome since 1984
spotlights.spot_it: Enormous floats and thousands of dancers in feathered costumes parading down a long stadium-lined avenue at night.
spotlights.story_md: Rio's carnival is both a street party and a fierce competition. The top samba schools, most rooted in poorer neighbourhoods and favelas, each parade once through the **Sambadrome**, a purpose-built avenue designed by architect **Oscar Niemeyer** and opened in **1984**. Each school gets a strict time window and is judged on categories including its drum section (bateria), costumes, floats and theme song. Schools spend most of the year building their show. Outside the stadium, hundreds of free street bands, called **blocos**, take over the city.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows carnival as a year-round community industry, not just a week of fun.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Rio the poorest neighbourhoods spend a year building one hour of glory.

spotlights.name: Notting Hill Carnival
spotlights.when: August bank holiday weekend; street event since 1966
spotlights.spot_it: Masqueraders in feathers and sequins, steel bands and sound systems moving through west London streets.
spotlights.story_md: After the racist riots in Notting Hill in **1958**, the Trinidad-born activist **Claudia Jones** organised an indoor Caribbean carnival in **1959** at St Pancras Town Hall to raise spirits and money. In **1966**, a local social worker, Rhaune Laslett, organised a street fair, and Caribbean musicians joined with a steel band. That became Notting Hill Carnival, now often described as Europe's largest street festival, with around **one to two million** people over two days. It has also been a site of conflict with police, most famously in 1976. It is a carnival born directly as a reply to racism.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a diaspora used a festival to claim space in a hostile city.
spotlights.memory_hook: Europe's biggest street party began as an answer to a race riot.

sections.title: Pain, rhythm and glue
sections.intro_md:
If festivals only felt good, they would be easy to explain. The puzzle is that many of them hurt. People walk on coals, pierce their cheeks with skewers, fast, carry heavy loads up hills, sleep in the cold on a riverbank for a month, or stand for 24 hours in a queue. Why would evolution leave us with a love of painful parties?

Psychologists now have three linked answers. First, **costly signals**: doing something painful or expensive for the group proves you are committed, in a way that cheap talk cannot. Second, **synchrony**: moving, singing or chanting in time with others seems to blur the line between self and group. In a 2009 experiment at Stanford, people who simply walked in step or sang together cooperated more afterwards in a money game. Third, **endorphins**: singing, dancing and laughing together release the brain's own opioids, which make us feel close to the people around us.

spotlights.name: Thaipusam and the kavadi
spotlights.when: Full moon of the Tamil month Thai (January to February)
spotlights.spot_it: Devotees in yellow carrying ornate arched frames (kavadi) fixed to their bodies by hooks and skewers, climbing towards a giant golden statue at Batu Caves.
spotlights.story_md: Thaipusam honours the god **Murugan** and is celebrated by Tamil communities in India, Malaysia, Singapore and Mauritius. Some devotees carry a **kavadi**, a decorated frame, and pierce their skin, tongue or cheeks with hooks and skewers. At **Batu Caves** near Kuala Lumpur, more than a million people gather, and pilgrims climb **272 steps**. In a **2013** study in Mauritius, Dimitris Xygalatas's team found that both people who performed the painful kavadi and those who watched it later gave more money anonymously to the temple than people who took part only in a low-pain prayer. The more pain people reported, the more they gave.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the strongest field evidence that shared ordeal can increase generosity.
spotlights.memory_hook: At Thaipusam, the bigger the skewer, the bigger the donation.

spotlights.name: The Magh Mela well-being study
spotlights.spot_it: A sea of tents and pilgrims on the sandy floodplain where the Ganga and Yamuna meet at Prayagraj, in winter mist.
spotlights.story_md: Every January and February, pilgrims called **kalpavasis** live for a month in tents on the riverbank at Prayagraj, bathing in near-freezing water, eating simply and sleeping amid noise and smoke. You would expect their health to suffer. Psychologists **Shruti Tewari, Sammyh Khan, Nick Hopkins, Narayanan Srinivasan and Stephen Reicher** followed **416 pilgrims** and **127 people** from the same villages who stayed home. A month after the Mela, the pilgrims reported **better** health and fewer aches and stress symptoms than before; the stay-at-homes did not change. The researchers credit **shared identity**: feeling part of a meaningful crowd makes hardship feel lighter.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It suggests mass festivals can be good for health, through belonging, not despite the crowd.
spotlights.memory_hook: A month in a freezing, noisy tent city left pilgrims healthier.

spotlights.name: Robin Dunbar and the ice-breaker effect
spotlights.spot_it: A white-haired British scientist, the man behind 'Dunbar's number', the idea that humans keep about 150 stable relationships.
spotlights.story_md: Oxford evolutionary psychologist **Robin Dunbar** argues that our ape ancestors bonded by grooming each other, one on one, but that human groups grew too big for that. Singing, dancing, feasting and laughing together, he says, are 'grooming at a distance': they trigger endorphins in many people at once. In a **2015** study, Eiluned Pearce, Jacques Launay and Dunbar followed adult evening classes in England over seven months. **Singing** classes bonded much faster at the start than crafts or creative writing classes. They called it the **ice-breaker effect**. By month seven, the other classes had caught up.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It gives a biological reason why almost every festival involves group singing and dancing.
spotlights.memory_hook: Singing together is grooming a hundred people at once.

sections.title: Giving it all away
sections.intro_md:
Economists have their own puzzle about festivals: why do people who are careful with money for eleven months spend recklessly in the twelfth? Indian families take loans for weddings and buy gold at Dhanteras. Christmas accounts for a huge share of annual retail sales in many Western countries. Some societies go further and destroy wealth on purpose.

The anthropological answer is that festive spending is not waste. It **converts money into status and relationships**. When you feed the whole village, you buy respect, alliances and future help. The French anthropologist **Marcel Mauss**, in his 1925 essay *The Gift*, argued that gifts are never free: they create obligations that bind people together. A festival is the moment when a society's whole web of obligation is refreshed in public.

Festivals also **redistribute**. In many places, the rich are expected to feed the poor at festival time. Langars, community feasts and charity at Eid (zakat al-fitr must be paid before the Eid prayer) all move food from those who have to those who do not. Below are three extreme cases, from British Columbia, Indonesia and India.

spotlights.name: The potlatch
spotlights.spot_it: A Pacific Northwest coast gathering with stacks of blankets, carved masks and painted copper shields displayed in a big house.
spotlights.story_md: Among the **Kwakwaka'wakw** and other peoples of the Pacific Northwest coast, a chief marked births, deaths, marriages and new titles with a **potlatch**: days of feasting, dancing and gift-giving in which he gave away blankets, canoes and food, and sometimes destroyed valuable 'coppers' or burned oil to show his wealth. Status came from what you gave, not what you kept. Canadian missionaries and officials saw it as wasteful and pagan, and an **1884** amendment to the Indian Act **banned** it from 1885. In **1921**, police raided a potlatch at Village Island, arrested dozens and seized masks and regalia. The ban was dropped in **1951**. Some seized objects were returned decades later.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows a festival can be an entire economic and political system, which is why a state tried to kill it.
spotlights.memory_hook: A chief's wealth was measured by what he gave away.

spotlights.name: Toraja funeral festivals
spotlights.when: Rambu Solo funerals; mostly in the dry season
spotlights.spot_it: Houses with dramatic upswept boat-shaped roofs, crowds in black, and water buffalo gathered for a funeral feast in the highlands of Sulawesi.
spotlights.story_md: In the **Toraja** highlands of Sulawesi, Indonesia, a death begins a long process. The body may stay at home for months or years, treated as 'sick' rather than dead, while the family saves for the funeral, called **Rambu Solo**. That funeral can last days, with hundreds of guests, and the sacrifice of **water buffalo** and pigs. A rare piebald buffalo can cost more than a car. The number of buffalo marks the family's status. Families may go into debt for a single funeral. In some villages, a later rite, **Ma'nene**, sees the dead taken out, cleaned and re-dressed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a festival for the dead doubles as a public ledger of family status.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Toraja, you save for your father's funeral the way others save for a house.

spotlights.name: Dhanteras and the festive economy
spotlights.spot_it: Crowded Indian market streets lit with lamps and lights, shoppers buying gold, silver coins and steel utensils.
spotlights.story_md: On **Dhanteras**, the first day of the five-day Diwali festival, many Hindu families buy gold, silver or a new metal utensil, a custom tied to wealth and the goddess Lakshmi. It anchors India's biggest spending season. The traders' body **CAIT** estimated Navratri-to-Diwali trade in **2025** at **₹6.05 lakh crore**, including ₹5.40 lakh crore in goods, about a quarter higher than its 2024 figure. That is a trade group's survey, not an audited number, but every retailer, carmaker and jeweller in India plans its year around it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows festivals are also the backbone of national retail calendars.
spotlights.memory_hook: Dhanteras: the one day a year buying a steel pot counts as worship.

sections.title: Inviting the dead to dinner
sections.intro_md:
Remember that the oldest feast we know was a funeral. That has not changed. Across the world, a large family of festivals exists so that the living can host the dead.

The pattern is remarkably consistent. Once a year, the boundary between worlds is said to thin. Families clean graves, cook the dead person's favourite food, light lamps or fires to guide them home, and then, after a few days, send them away again. China has **Qingming** and the Hungry Ghost Festival, Japan has **Obon**, Hindus observe **Pitru Paksha**, Catholic countries mark All Souls, and Mexico has **Día de Muertos**.

Psychologists see these as a social technology for grief. They give mourning a schedule, so that sorrow has a place to go each year, and they keep the dead inside the family story. They also teach children who their great-grandparents were. A festival for the dead is, in practice, a festival of family memory, which is why even very secular families tend to keep them.

spotlights.name: Día de Muertos
spotlights.spot_it: Home altars (ofrendas) stacked with orange marigolds, candles, photos of the dead, sugar skulls and loaves of pan de muerto.
spotlights.story_md: In Mexico, families believe the dead return to visit on **1 and 2 November**. They build **ofrendas**, altars with photos, the dead person's favourite food and drink, candles, and bright orange **cempasúchil** (marigolds), whose smell and colour are said to guide souls home. Cemeteries fill with families eating and playing music at the graves. UNESCO listed the tradition in **2008**. The big Mexico City parade is a recent addition: it was invented for the James Bond film **Spectre** (2015), and the city created a real one in **2016** because tourists kept asking for it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a festival for the dead can be joyful, and how fast new customs get added.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mexico City's Day of the Dead parade was copied from a James Bond film.

spotlights.name: Obon
spotlights.when: Mid-August in most of Japan (July in some regions)
spotlights.spot_it: Paper lanterns floating on a dark river; circles of people in summer kimono dancing slowly around a raised drum tower.
spotlights.story_md: During **Obon**, Japanese families believe the spirits of ancestors come home for a few days. They clean graves, light lanterns at the door, and offer food. Towns hold **Bon Odori**, simple circle dances anyone can join, around a tower with taiko drums. At the end, families send the spirits back with fires or by floating lanterns down rivers (**tōrō nagashi**). In Kyoto, giant bonfire characters are lit on the mountains around the city on 16 August. Obon is also Japan's biggest holiday travel period, its own small version of China's Chunyun.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the welcome-and-send-away structure of nearly all festivals of the dead.
spotlights.memory_hook: Obon: light a lantern to call them home, float one to send them back.

spotlights.name: Pitru Paksha and pind daan at Gaya
spotlights.when: 16 lunar days in Bhadrapada (September to October)
spotlights.spot_it: Men with shaved heads in white dhotis offering balls of rice and sesame at a riverbank, guided by priests, at Gaya in Bihar.
spotlights.story_md: **Pitru Paksha**, the 'fortnight of the ancestors', is when Hindus perform **shraddha** for three generations of dead forebears, offering **pinda**, balls of cooked rice mixed with sesame and ghee. Crows are fed because they are believed to carry offerings to the dead. **Gaya** in Bihar, on the Phalgu river, is the most important place for these rites, and its Vishnupad temple draws lakhs of people in the season. The fortnight is considered inauspicious for new purchases. It ends on **Mahalaya**, which in Bengal also marks the start of the Durga Puja season.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is India's great festival of the dead, and a hinge into its biggest festival season.
spotlights.memory_hook: For two weeks a year, Hindu families feed their great-grandparents through the crows.

sections.title: Light against the dark
sections.intro_md:
Look at a list of the world's best-loved festivals and an astonishing number are about **lamps**. Diwali's diyas, Hanukkah's candles, St Lucia's crown of flames, China's lanterns, Thailand's floating lights, Christmas lights on every high street.

The simplest explanation is physical. Most of them cluster in the dark half of the year, near the winter solstice in the northern hemisphere, when nights are long and spirits low. Before electricity, light was expensive. Burning a lot of it at once was a luxury that announced abundance and defiance at the same time.

The deeper explanation is symbolic. Almost every tradition uses light for knowledge, goodness, safety and life, and darkness for the opposite. A festival of lights turns an abstract hope into something you can do with your hands: fill a lamp, light a wick, put it in a window where your neighbours can see it. That visibility matters. A lit window says this household belongs.

spotlights.name: Diwali
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of small clay oil lamps (diyas) along doorsteps and balconies, with rangoli patterns on the floor, on a moonless night.
spotlights.story_md: **Diwali** is a five-day festival held on the darkest night of the Hindu month of Kartik. For many Hindus it marks the return of **Rama** to Ayodhya; for others it honours **Lakshmi** or Kali. Jains mark the nirvana of **Mahavira**, Sikhs observe **Bandi Chhor Divas**, the release of Guru Hargobind, and Newar Buddhists celebrate it too. Homes are cleaned, lamps lit, sweets shared and fireworks set off. On **10 December 2025**, UNESCO inscribed **Deepavali** on its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity at a meeting held at Delhi's **Red Fort**. It is India's 16th element on that list.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the clearest case of one festival carrying several religions' meanings at once.
spotlights.memory_hook: Diwali: four religions, one lamp.

spotlights.name: Hanukkah
spotlights.spot_it: A nine-branched candlestick (hanukkiah) in a window, with one more candle lit each night by a helper candle.
spotlights.story_md: **Hanukkah** marks the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem in **164 BCE**, after the Maccabees revolted against the Seleucid Greek king who had banned Jewish practice. The famous story of a single day's oil that burned for **eight days** does not appear in the Books of Maccabees; it is first recorded in the **Talmud**, centuries later. Families light one more candle each night on a nine-branched lamp, the ninth being the **shamash** helper, and traditionally place it in a window to 'publicise the miracle'. Fried foods, latkes and doughnuts, honour the oil.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a festival's best-known story can arrive centuries after the event.
spotlights.memory_hook: Eight nights of light from oil that was only meant to last one.

spotlights.name: St Lucia's Day
spotlights.spot_it: A girl in a white gown with a red sash and a crown of lit candles leads a procession of singers carrying candles.
spotlights.story_md: On **13 December** in Sweden, a girl chosen as **Lucia** wears a crown of candles and leads a candlelit procession singing, followed by attendants and 'star boys', and everyone eats saffron buns. Under the old Julian calendar, 13 December fell close to the **winter solstice**, the longest night. Lucia was a Christian martyr from Sicily, but the Swedish procession is mostly modern: it spread nationally after a Stockholm newspaper ran a Lucia contest in **1927**. Battery candles are now common in schools.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how an old saint's day became a modern national light festival.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sweden's darkest morning is greeted by a girl wearing a crown on fire.

sections.title: Permission to make a mess
sections.intro_md:
Some festivals exist mainly to let adults do what children are scolded for: throw things, get filthy, soak strangers, and scream with laughter. Tomatoes, oranges, water, coloured powder, mud, flour, even rotten eggs have all been official festival weapons.

Why? Messy festivals do several jobs at once. They **dissolve status**: once everyone is purple or dripping, you cannot tell the boss from the cleaner. They **lower inhibition**: hitting a stranger with powder is a forced, harmless introduction. They **mark a season**: Holi and Songkran are both spring festivals in hot countries, and water and colour suit the moment.

Many of these festivals also have a quiet rule-book underneath the chaos. Holi colour is played after the solemn bonfire of the night before. La Tomatina has a starting signal, an end signal and a rule that tomatoes must be squashed before being thrown. Ivrea's battle has teams, a uniform for spectators and a legend to justify it. Licensed chaos is still licensed.

spotlights.name: Holi
spotlights.spot_it: Crowds drenched in pink, green and yellow powder; in Barsana, women swinging long sticks at men holding shields.
spotlights.story_md: **Holi** marks the arrival of spring. It begins the night before with **Holika Dahan**, a bonfire for the story of the demoness Holika burned while the child devotee Prahlad survived. The next morning, people throw coloured powder and water at friends and strangers. Around Mathura, the festival lasts days and reenacts stories of **Krishna** and **Radha**. In **Lathmar Holi** at **Barsana**, women beat men from Krishna's village of Nandgaon with long sticks, and the men protect themselves with shields, recalling Krishna's teasing of Radha's friends. Colours were traditionally made from flowers such as palash (tesu).
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows a festival dissolving rank and gender roles for a day.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Barsana, the women carry the sticks.

spotlights.name: La Tomatina
spotlights.spot_it: A narrow Spanish street ankle-deep in red tomato pulp, packed with people in goggles and white T-shirts turned red.
spotlights.story_md: La Tomatina began in **1945** in **Buñol**, near Valencia, when young men started a scuffle during a parade and grabbed tomatoes from a stall to throw. They did it again the next year, and the town tried to ban it in the 1950s; a mock 'tomato funeral' protest in **1957** helped bring it back. Since **2013** it has been a paid, capped event. In **2025** about **22,000** people threw roughly **120 tonnes** of tomatoes in about an hour. Rules: squash tomatoes before throwing, do not tear shirts, stop at the second signal. Fire engines hose the streets afterwards.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a one-off prank can become a tradition in a single generation.
spotlights.memory_hook: Buñol's tomato fight started as a brawl and got a mock funeral when it was banned.

spotlights.name: The Battle of the Oranges
spotlights.when: Carnival, the days before Lent; Ivrea, Italy
spotlights.spot_it: Teams on foot in coloured jerseys pelting horse-drawn carts of masked, helmeted throwers with oranges, the cobbles slick with juice.
spotlights.story_md: At carnival in **Ivrea**, in Piedmont, teams on foot represent the townspeople and throw oranges at people on carts who play the tyrant's guards. The legend is that a miller's daughter, **Violetta**, beheaded a medieval lord who claimed a 'right' to her on her wedding night, sparking a revolt. Spectators wear a red stocking cap to show they are not fighting. Reported totals of oranges range from about **250 to nearly 1,000 tonnes**, depending on the year and how they are counted. Injuries are common, mostly bruises and eye injuries.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows carnival turning a story of rebellion against a lord into a yearly ritual battle.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Ivrea, revolution is reenacted with fruit.

sections.title: The biggest crowds in history
sections.intro_md:
The largest gatherings our species has ever assembled are not sports finals or protests. They are pilgrimages tied to festival dates. Three of the top contenders happen within a few hours' flight of each other: the **Kumbh Mela** in India, **Arbaeen** in Iraq and the **Hajj** in Saudi Arabia.

These gatherings stretch every system a state has: water, sanitation, rail, policing, medical care, food. Saudi Arabia limits the Hajj by **quotas** for each country. Iraq relies on thousands of volunteer roadside kitchens called **mawkibs** to feed Arbaeen walkers for free.

Counting is genuinely hard. Officials have political reasons to report big numbers, and methods range from drones and AI cameras to crude estimates. Treat every figure here as an order of magnitude. What nobody disputes is that hundreds of millions of people are willing to travel, often at great cost and some risk, to stand in the same place at the same time as everyone else.

visual.title: Reported attendance at the largest gatherings (millions)

spotlights.name: Kumbh Mela
spotlights.when: Rotates among four river cities; Maha Kumbh at Prayagraj, 13 January to 26 February 2025
spotlights.spot_it: Endless rows of tents and pontoon bridges on a sandy floodplain, ash-smeared naga sadhus running into the river at dawn.
spotlights.story_md: The **Kumbh Mela** rotates among **Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain and Nashik**, returning to each roughly every 12 years by an astrological cycle. The story is that drops of the nectar of immortality fell at these four places. The 2025 **Maha Kumbh** at Prayagraj ran **45 days**; the Uttar Pradesh government said **66.21 crore** (662 million) people bathed, a number impossible to check independently. UNESCO listed the Kumbh in **2017**. Mark Twain visited the Magh Mela at the same spot in **1895** and wrote that it was wonderful, the power of a faith like that, to make multitudes travel so far.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the largest peaceful gathering of humans ever recorded.
spotlights.memory_hook: A city the size of a country that exists for six weeks on a riverbed.

spotlights.name: Hajj
spotlights.spot_it: Pilgrims in plain white unstitched cloth circling the black-draped Kaaba in Mecca, or standing on the plain of Arafat.
spotlights.story_md: The **Hajj** is one of the five pillars of Islam, required once in a lifetime of every adult Muslim who can afford it and is able. For five days, pilgrims follow the same route: circling the **Kaaba**, standing in prayer on the plain of **Arafat**, stoning pillars representing the devil at **Mina**. Men wear the **ihram**, two plain white sheets, so that a king and a labourer look alike, which is Victor Turner's communitas made visible. Saudi statistics counted **1,707,301** pilgrims in **2026**, up about 2% on 2025. Countries receive quotas, and India's runs into the lakhs.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows a festival deliberately designed to erase visible rank.
spotlights.memory_hook: On Hajj, two white sheets make every man the same.

spotlights.name: Arbaeen
spotlights.spot_it: Millions of people dressed mostly in black walking along a highway towards the golden domes of Karbala, past roadside tents serving food.
spotlights.story_md: **Arbaeen** marks the 40th day after **Ashura**, the anniversary of the killing of **Husayn ibn Ali**, the Prophet's grandson, at Karbala in **680 CE**. Shia Muslims walk to Karbala, many from Najaf about **80 km** away, some from Basra or Iran. Along the road, volunteers run thousands of **mawkibs**, tents offering free food, tea, beds and even foot massages. The Al-Abbas shrine's camera count claimed **21,103,524** pilgrims in **2025**. That figure is not independently verified, but even sceptics agree Arbaeen is among the largest annual gatherings on Earth.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows a festival economy run almost entirely on free giving.
spotlights.memory_hook: On the road to Karbala, nobody pays for dinner.

spotlights.name: Rath Yatra, Puri
spotlights.spot_it: Three giant wooden temple chariots with striped canopies being hauled by thousands of people on ropes down a wide street.
spotlights.story_md: Once a year, the deities **Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra** leave their temple in **Puri**, Odisha, and ride three huge chariots, rebuilt from fresh wood every year, about **3 km** to the Gundicha temple. Anyone, of any caste, may pull the ropes. Before the chariots move, the Gajapati king of Puri sweeps them with a golden broom, a ritual of royal humility. Jagannath's chariot gave English the word **juggernaut**, from colonial-era reports of devotees crushed under its wheels, much exaggerated. In **June 2025**, a crush near the Gundicha temple killed **three** people.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows a deity coming out to the people, and a king acting as a sweeper.
spotlights.memory_hook: Juggernaut began as a chariot in Puri.

sections.title: India's festival machine
sections.intro_md:
India may be the world's most festive country by sheer count. Every major religion is present, every state has its own harvest and new year festivals, and many villages have a local deity with its own fair. The lunar calendar shifts dates every year, so planning offices, railways, schools and stock markets all publish festival calendars.

Three Indian lessons stand out. First, festivals map onto farming. **Bihu** in Assam has three versions, for sowing, for the lean season and for harvest. **Pongal** and **Onam** are harvest thanksgivings. Second, festivals can be **political inventions**. The public Ganesh festival in Maharashtra was turned into a mass event in the 1890s for nationalist ends; Nagaland's **Hornbill Festival** was created by the state government in 2000. Third, festivals are a **creative economy**: a 2019 British Council study put the value of creative work around Durga Puja in West Bengal at about **₹32,377 crore**, roughly 2.6% of the state's GDP.

spotlights.name: Ganesh Chaturthi as a public festival
spotlights.when: Bhadrapada (August to September); public form from the 1890s
spotlights.spot_it: Towering Ganesh idols in street pandals; on the last day, huge processions with drums carry them to the sea for immersion.
spotlights.story_md: Ganesh worship at home is old, but the giant **public** festival is modern. In the early **1890s** in Pune, the nationalist **Bal Gangadhar Tilak** promoted community (sarvajanik) Ganesh celebrations, partly because British rules made political meetings hard while religious gatherings were tolerated. Pune's Bhausaheb Rangari is also credited with an earlier public Ganesh in 1892, and the two claims are still debated. The festival now lasts up to ten days and ends with immersion (**visarjan**). In Mumbai, the **Lalbaugcha Raja** idol, set up since **1934**, draws queues that last more than a day.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a textbook case of a domestic ritual turned into a mass political festival.
spotlights.memory_hook: Tilak turned a household god into a street-corner rally.

spotlights.name: Bal Gangadhar Tilak
spotlights.spot_it: A stern man with a heavy moustache, a red Puneri pagadi turban and a shawl.
spotlights.story_md: Tilak, called **Lokmanya** ('accepted by the people'), was one of the first leaders to demand full self-rule, famous for the line 'Swaraj is my birthright, and I shall have it'. He understood that festivals could gather crowds the colonial state could not easily stop. He promoted public **Ganeshotsav** from the 1890s and the **Shivaji festival** from 1896, using songs, plays and speeches at both to spread nationalist ideas. The British jailed him several times, including six years in Mandalay. His strategy shows one more reason humans have festivals: they are a lawful way to assemble.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He showed how festivals can be turned into political organising tools.
spotlights.memory_hook: Tilak's loudspeaker was a festival.

spotlights.name: Durga Puja in Kolkata
spotlights.spot_it: A ten-armed goddess on a lion, slaying a buffalo demon, inside a temporary pandal that may imitate a temple, a palace or an art installation.
spotlights.story_md: Bengal's **Durga Puja** celebrates the goddess Durga's victory over the buffalo demon **Mahishasura** and, in Bengali tradition, her visit home to her parents. Clay idols are sculpted by artisans in **Kumartuli**, north Kolkata. Thousands of community pandals compete on design, many now works of contemporary art, and crowds walk all night 'pandal-hopping'. UNESCO inscribed **Durga Puja in Kolkata** in **December 2021**. A British Council study estimated the festival's creative economy at about **₹32,377 crore** in 2019. On the last day, married women smear each other with vermilion (**sindoor khela**) before the idols are immersed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows a religious festival that is also a city's biggest art exhibition and industry.
spotlights.memory_hook: For five days, Kolkata becomes one huge open-air gallery.

spotlights.name: Onam
spotlights.spot_it: Circular carpets of flower petals (pookalam) in front of homes; a long banana-leaf feast with many small dishes.
spotlights.story_md: Onam is Kerala's harvest festival and celebrates the yearly return of **Mahabali**, a generous demon king whose rule was so just that the gods grew jealous. Vishnu, as the dwarf **Vamana**, pushed him into the underworld but allowed him to visit his people once a year. Families make **pookalam** flower carpets that grow larger each of the ten days, and eat the **sadya**, a vegetarian feast of more than 20 dishes served on a banana leaf. Snake-boat races (**vallam kali**) with crews of about 100 rowers take place on the backwaters. Onam is celebrated across religions in Kerala.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows a festival that remembers a golden age and invites its lost king home.
spotlights.memory_hook: Once a year, Kerala lays a flower carpet for a banished king.

spotlights.name: Hornbill Festival
spotlights.spot_it: Naga warriors in red and black shawls, feathered headgear and bead necklaces dancing in a heritage village of traditional houses.
spotlights.story_md: The **Hornbill Festival** is held at **Kisama Heritage Village** near Kohima, starting on Nagaland's statehood day, **1 December**. The state government created it in **2000** to bring Nagaland's tribes together in one place and to promote tourism. Each tribe has a traditional house (morung) in the village and performs its own dances, songs and games. It is named after the great hornbill, a bird whose feathers appear in Naga headdresses. Barely 25 years old, it already feels traditional, which makes it a perfect example of an invented festival that works.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that a government can build a festival from scratch and make it stick.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hornbill: a festival younger than most of its visitors.

spotlights.name: Bihu
spotlights.when: Three Bihus: April, October and January
spotlights.spot_it: Young dancers in cream and red muga silk mekhela chadors, swaying with raised arms to the dhol and pepa horn.
spotlights.story_md: Assam's **Bihu** is three festivals that track the farming year. **Rongali** or Bohag Bihu (mid-April) is the new year and sowing season, full of the energetic Bihu dance and songs. **Kongali** or Kati Bihu (October) comes in the lean months when granaries are empty; people light lamps in the fields and at the tulsi plant. **Bhogali** or Magh Bihu (January) is the harvest feast, with community bonfires (**meji**) and huts that are burned at dawn. The happy, sober and feasting Bihus are a calendar of moods.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how festivals encode a farming year's hopes, worries and plenty.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bihu has three moods: hope, hunger, feast.

spotlights.name: Pongal
spotlights.spot_it: A clay pot of rice and milk boiling over on an open fire in front of a kolam drawing, decorated with turmeric plants and sugarcane.
spotlights.story_md: **Pongal** is the Tamil harvest festival at the start of the month of Thai, when the sun begins its northward journey. The name means 'boiling over'. Families cook new rice in milk and jaggery in a new pot, and when it bubbles over everyone shouts **'Pongalo Pongal'**, a sign of abundance. The day before, Bhogi, old things are burned. On **Mattu Pongal**, cattle are washed, their horns painted, and they are fed and honoured; in some districts this is also the time of **Jallikattu**, bull-taming.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows a festival that thanks the sun, the soil and the animals that work it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pongal: the one day a pot is supposed to overflow.

sections.title: Invented yesterday
sections.intro_md:
Many festivals feel ancient but are surprisingly new. In **1983** the historians **Eric Hobsbawm** and **Terence Ranger** edited a book called *The Invention of Tradition*, which showed that many 'timeless' British customs, from royal pageantry to the Scottish clan tartan, were created in the 18th and 19th centuries, often to give a new nation or institution a feeling of age.

Festivals are a prime case. The Christmas many people know, with a tree, Santa, stockings and a family dinner, was largely assembled in the 19th century by writers, illustrators and a royal family. Mother's Day, Kwanzaa, Singles' Day and Nagaland's Hornbill Festival were all founded by identifiable people within living memory.

This is not cynical. The need for festivals is so strong that when old ones fade, people invent fresh ones, and within a generation they feel traditional.

spotlights.name: The royal Christmas tree, 1848
spotlights.spot_it: A Victorian engraving of Queen Victoria, Prince Albert and their children gathered round a candle-lit tabletop fir tree hung with gifts.
spotlights.story_md: Decorated evergreen trees were a German custom. Queen Victoria's German-born husband, **Prince Albert**, set them up at Windsor, and in **December 1848** the *Illustrated London News* printed an engraving of the royal family around one. Middle-class Britain copied it. In **1850** the American magazine *Godey's Lady's Book* reprinted the picture with a twist: the editors removed Victoria's tiara and Albert's moustache so the family looked like ordinary Americans. Within a generation the Christmas tree became standard in both countries.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how one widely printed image can create a 'tradition' within years.
spotlights.memory_hook: America's Christmas tree came from a royal picture with the crown erased.

spotlights.name: Thomas Nast's Santa Claus
spotlights.spot_it: A round, white-bearded, jolly man in a fur-trimmed suit with a pipe and a sack of toys, in black-and-white engravings.
spotlights.story_md: The German-born cartoonist **Thomas Nast** drew Santa Claus for *Harper's Weekly* for over 20 years, starting with 'Santa Claus in Camp' in **January 1863**, where Santa hands out gifts to Union soldiers in the Civil War. Nast gave Santa his workshop, his North Pole home and his list of good and bad children. His 1881 'Merry Old Santa Claus' fixed the modern look. A popular myth says **Coca-Cola** invented the red-suited Santa in its 1930s ads by Haddon Sundblom. It did not: red Santas appeared decades earlier, although Coca-Cola's ads did help standardise the image.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a festival's central figure was designed by illustrators and publishers.
spotlights.memory_hook: Santa's North Pole address was a cartoonist's idea.

spotlights.name: Anna Jarvis and Mother's Day
spotlights.spot_it: A serious woman in early 20th-century dress; the festival's emblem was a white carnation.
spotlights.story_md: **Anna Jarvis** organised the first Mother's Day service in **Grafton, West Virginia**, in **1908**, to honour her own mother. She campaigned until President Woodrow Wilson made it a national day in **1914**. Then florists, card companies and confectioners turned it into a sales event, and Jarvis spent the rest of her life and fortune fighting them. She was arrested in **1925** for disrupting a convention selling carnations. She died poor in a sanatorium in 1948. Her story is the purest example of a founder losing her festival to the market.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how quickly a new festival becomes a commercial one.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mother's Day's founder ended up campaigning against Mother's Day.

spotlights.name: Kwanzaa
spotlights.spot_it: A seven-branched candleholder (kinara) with three red, one black and three green candles, on a mat with fruit and an ear of corn.
spotlights.story_md: **Maulana Karenga**, a Black activist and professor, created **Kwanzaa** in **1966**, after the Watts uprising in Los Angeles, as a specifically African American holiday. The name comes from the Swahili phrase for 'first fruits'. Each of its seven days is devoted to one of seven principles, the **Nguzo Saba**, such as unity and collective work, and a candle is lit on the **kinara**. It borrows from African harvest festivals but is openly new. That openness is part of its point: a community without inherited holidays it felt were its own made one.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows people deliberately designing a festival to build identity.
spotlights.memory_hook: Kwanzaa: a harvest festival invented in Los Angeles.

spotlights.name: Singles' Day (11.11)
spotlights.spot_it: Giant screens counting sales in real time, red '11.11' logos, and courier depots overflowing with parcels.
spotlights.story_md: The date **11 November**, written 11.11, looks like four single people. Students at **Nanjing University** reportedly began marking it as an anti-Valentine's Day in the **1990s**. In **2009**, Alibaba turned it into an online sale with 27 merchants. By **2021**, Alibaba reported gross merchandise value of about **540 billion yuan** over the extended festival, and it then stopped publishing the figure. It is probably the biggest shopping event in the world, and a festival with no religion, no season and no history beyond a student joke.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that a festival can be born from a date's shape and grown by a company.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four ones on a calendar became the world's biggest shopping day.

sections.title: The secular pilgrimage
sections.intro_md:
In the 20th century, many people in industrial countries stopped going to religious festivals. They did not stop gathering. Music festivals, sports tournaments, fan conventions and city light shows filled the gap, and sociologists have noticed that they borrow almost every feature of the old festivals.

There is a **pilgrimage**: a long trip, often uncomfortable, to a special place. There is **liminality**: camping in a field, wearing costumes or wristbands, staying up all night. There is **communitas**: strangers share food, sing the same songs and feel equal. There are **relics** (ticket stubs, wristbands, mud-caked boots) and even **saints** (headliners whose sets become legend).

The psychologist's measurements apply too. Studies of football crowds and concerts find the same synchrony and shared-identity effects as studies of religious rituals. The difference is that secular festivals are sold as tickets, and that changes who can come.

spotlights.name: Woodstock
spotlights.spot_it: A vast crowd on a sloping green dairy farm field facing a distant wooden stage, with tents, mud and hand-painted signs.
spotlights.story_md: The Woodstock Music and Art Fair was held on **Max Yasgur's dairy farm** in **Bethel, New York**, about 70 km from the town of Woodstock. Organisers expected far fewer people; about **400,000** came, fences went down and it became a free festival. Roads jammed, food ran short and rain turned the field to mud. Local people and the farm's neighbours fed strangers. Jimi Hendrix closed the festival on Monday morning to a crowd that had shrunk to tens of thousands. Woodstock became a symbol of a whole generation, partly because the film of it reached millions who were not there.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It became the model of the modern music festival as a secular pilgrimage.
spotlights.memory_hook: Half a million people, one farm, three days of rain.

spotlights.name: Glastonbury Festival
spotlights.spot_it: A large pyramid-shaped stage in a valley of tents and flags, with crowds of tens of thousands in the evening.
spotlights.story_md: Dairy farmer **Michael Eavis** held the first festival at **Worthy Farm**, Somerset, on **19 September 1970**, the day after Jimi Hendrix died. Tickets cost **£1**, including free milk from the farm, and about **1,500** people came. Today about **200,000** people attend, tickets sell out in under an hour, and the farm still takes regular **fallow years** to let the land and the village rest. The festival gives millions to charities. It is a working farm that becomes one of England's biggest towns for five days each June.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the rhythm of a festival: a temporary city, then a rest.
spotlights.memory_hook: Glastonbury started with a £1 ticket and a free pint of milk.

sections.title: When festivals hurt
sections.intro_md:
A clear-eyed day on festivals has to count their costs. Large crowds in tight spaces are dangerous, and the history of mass gatherings is also a history of **crowd crushes**. Crowd scientists such as **G. Keith Still** stress that crushes are mostly failures of design and management, not 'stampedes' of panicking people. When density passes about five or six people per square metre, individuals can no longer control their movement, and pressure waves can kill people standing still.

Recent Indian examples include the **Maha Kumbh** crush of **29 January 2025**, where the official toll of 37 was challenged by a BBC investigation that documented at least 82 deaths, and the **Puri Rath Yatra** crush of **June 2025**, which killed three.

Festivals carry other costs. **Firecrackers** at Diwali push Delhi's already severe autumn air pollution higher, which is why the Supreme Court has restricted firecracker sales in the region since 2017. Heat is a growing danger at Hajj. Even the family feast has a measurable cost: a Swedish study of 283,014 heart attacks found risk was **37% higher on Christmas Eve**, peaking around **10 pm**.

spotlights.name: The 2015 Mina crush
spotlights.spot_it: A valley filled with tens of thousands of identical white fireproof tents near Mecca, and the multi-level Jamarat bridge where pilgrims throw pebbles.
spotlights.story_md: On **24 September 2015**, during the Hajj, two flows of pilgrims met at a street junction in **Mina**, on the way to the stoning ritual at the Jamarat. Saudi authorities gave an official toll of **769** dead. Counts compiled by news agencies from the governments of pilgrims' home countries came to more than **2,400**, which would make it the deadliest Hajj disaster ever. After earlier disasters at the bridge, Saudi Arabia had rebuilt the Jamarat as a multi-level structure. The 2015 crush happened on an approach street, showing that crowd safety depends on the whole route, not one building.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how the same crowd that creates communitas can turn deadly when flows are mismanaged.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two crowds meeting at one junction killed more people than many wars.

spotlights.name: Diwali smoke in Delhi
spotlights.when: Late October to November each year
spotlights.spot_it: India Gate and Rajpath hazy grey in thick smog; night skies over Delhi lit by fireworks.
spotlights.story_md: Delhi's air is at its worst in late autumn, when still, cool air traps pollution near the ground and crop stubble burns in Punjab and Haryana. Diwali falls in exactly that window, and a night of firecrackers adds a sharp spike of fine particles and smoke. The **Supreme Court** first banned firecracker sales in Delhi-NCR in **2017**, later allowing only 'green' crackers on fixed hours in some years. Enforcement has been patchy and the debate is fierce, because crackers carry cultural meaning and jobs, especially in **Sivakasi**, Tamil Nadu, the centre of India's fireworks industry.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows a festival tradition colliding with a public-health emergency.
spotlights.memory_hook: Diwali's lamps are ancient; its smoke problem is modern.

sections.title: Myths, tested
sections.intro_md:
Festivals attract stories, and some of the best-known ones do not survive a check. The table below sets out common claims against what the evidence shows.

A general rule helps. Be suspicious of any claim that a festival is 'really' an older pagan one in disguise. Festivals do borrow from each other, but the borrowing is usually partial, contested and slow. Christmas falling near the solstice may reflect the Roman sun cult, or a Christian calculation from the date of the Annunciation, or both; historians still disagree. Likewise be suspicious of very precise attendance figures for vast gatherings; they are estimates, often political.

The truth is usually layered: old instincts, older materials and a recent re-design.

data.evidence: Red Santas appear in the 19th and early 20th centuries; Coca-Cola's 1931 ads helped standardise the look.

data.claim: Christmas is on 25 December because of a pagan sun festival
data.evidence: Sol Invictus theory and a Christian date-calculation theory both have support.

data.claim: The Maya built Chichén Itzá to make an equinox snake
data.evidence: The effect is real but lasts weeks; no Maya source describes it.

data.claim: The Hanukkah oil miracle is in the Books of Maccabees
data.evidence: It is first recorded in the Talmud, centuries later.

data.claim: Devotees routinely threw themselves under Jagannath's chariot
data.evidence: Colonial accounts inflated rare deaths into the word 'juggernaut'.

data.claim: Mexico City's Day of the Dead parade is an ancient custom
data.evidence: First held in 2016, after the 2015 James Bond film Spectre.

data.claim: Festival crowds die because people panic and stampede
data.evidence: Most deaths come from crowd density and poor flow design, not panic.

sections.title: What is happening now, 2025 to 2026
sections.intro_md:
The last two years have been a reminder of how big, how political and how risky festivals have become.

India staged the largest gathering in recorded history at the **2025 Maha Kumbh**, and also faced hard questions about counting both crowds and the dead. UNESCO added **Deepavali** to its heritage list at a session India hosted at the **Red Fort** in December 2025, the first time India hosted the committee. China's Spring Festival travel rush set another record in early 2026. The Hajj grew slightly. Preparations for the **2027 Simhastha Kumbh** at Nashik and Trimbakeshwar are well under way, with a state authority approving about ₹9,600 crore of works.

Festivals are growing, not shrinking, as incomes rise and travel gets cheaper. The question for the next decade is less whether people will keep gathering and more whether states can keep gatherings of tens of millions safe, clean and honestly counted.

sections.title: So why do humans have festivals?
sections.intro_md:
There is no single answer, and that is the answer. Festivals survive because they do many jobs at once, and any one of them would be reason enough.

They **keep time**, pinning the year to the sun, moon and harvest. They **bind groups**, through synchrony, shared emotion and Durkheim's effervescence, measurable in heartbeats. They **prove commitment**, through costly gifts and painful ordeals that cheap talk cannot fake. They **move people across thresholds**, from one year, age or status to the next. They **release pressure**, letting a hierarchy laugh at itself so it can carry on. They **redistribute** wealth and refresh the web of gifts and debts. They **honour the dead**, giving grief a calendar. And they **build identity**, which is why states, movements and companies keep inventing new ones.

The table sums up the six main theories you met today. The next time you light a diya, carry a kavadi, dance at a wedding or queue for a concert, try to spot which jobs that festival is doing. Usually it is most of them.

visual.title: Six theories of why festivals exist

data.in_one_line: The crowd's shared emotion makes the group feel real and sacred.
Festivals move people across thresholds and make them feel equal while in between.
Licensed disorder lets a society mock its order, and often survive it.
Festive giving creates obligations that bind people and rank them.
Shared ordeal and moving in time build trust and generosity.
New groups and states make new festivals that quickly feel ancient.
