best_facts.fact: The oldest clear feast we know, about 12,000 years ago in a cave in Israel, was a funeral: at least 71 tortoises and three wild cattle were eaten around a woman buried as a shaman.
best_facts.why_surprising: The first party on record is a wake.

best_facts.fact: At a Spanish fire-walking festival, the heart rates of fire-walkers synchronised with their friends and relatives in the crowd, but not with unrelated spectators sitting in the same stands.
best_facts.why_surprising: Festival 'togetherness' shows up on a heart monitor, and it is selective.

best_facts.fact: Pilgrims who spent a month in cold, smoky, crowded tents at the Magh Mela in Prayagraj reported better health afterwards than neighbours who stayed home.
best_facts.why_surprising: Hardship plus a crowd made people healthier.

best_facts.fact: Mexico City's Day of the Dead parade was invented for the 2015 James Bond film Spectre; the city began staging a real one in 2016.
best_facts.why_surprising: An 'ancient' festival scene was copied from Hollywood.

best_facts.fact: In Babylon's new year festival, the high priest slapped the king's face; if he cried, the god was pleased.
best_facts.why_surprising: The most powerful man in the city was humiliated on schedule.

best_facts.fact: At Thaipusam in Mauritius, people who pierced themselves for the kavadi, and even those who only watched, later gave more money to the temple than people at a painless prayer.
Pigs eaten at Durrington Walls near Stonehenge around 2500 BCE were raised as far away as Scotland and Wales and driven hundreds of kilometres to midwinter feasts.
best_facts.why_surprising: Neolithic Britons travelled across the island for a barbecue.

best_facts.fact: Anna Jarvis, who founded Mother's Day in 1908, spent the rest of her life fighting it and was arrested in 1925 for disrupting a carnation sale.
best_facts.why_surprising: The founder became the festival's fiercest critic.

best_facts.fact: Canada banned the potlatch, a gift-giving feast, from 1885 to 1951, and in 1921 police raided one and seized its masks.
best_facts.why_surprising: A state outlawed a party for giving too much away.

best_facts.fact: When an American magazine reprinted the 1848 picture of Queen Victoria's Christmas tree, it erased her tiara and Prince Albert's moustache to make them look American.
best_facts.why_surprising: America's Christmas tree tradition began with a doctored royal photo-op.

best_facts.fact: Tilak promoted public Ganesh festivals in the 1890s partly because religious gatherings could assemble crowds that political meetings could not.
best_facts.why_surprising: Mumbai's biggest festival began as a workaround to colonial rules.

best_facts.fact: The English word 'juggernaut' comes from Jagannath's chariot at the Puri Rath Yatra.
best_facts.why_surprising: An everyday English word is a Hindu god's name.

best_facts.fact: Swedish heart-attack risk rises about 37% on Christmas Eve, peaking around 10 pm.
best_facts.why_surprising: The family feast has a measurable medical cost.

best_facts.fact: The Hanukkah story of one day's oil burning for eight days is not in the Books of Maccabees; it first appears in the Talmud, centuries later.
best_facts.why_surprising: The festival's best-known story is a later addition.

best_facts.fact: Newgrange in Ireland, older than the Great Pyramid, lets the winter-solstice sunrise light its inner chamber for about 17 minutes a year.
best_facts.why_surprising: A 5,000-year-old building engineered for one annual moment.

best_facts.fact: China's 2026 Spring Festival travel rush logged 9.41 billion inter-regional trips in 40 days.
best_facts.why_surprising: More than six trips per Chinese person, for one holiday.

best_facts.fact: The first Glastonbury Festival in 1970 cost £1, including free milk from the farm.
best_facts.why_surprising: A festival of 200,000 began as a dairy farmer's side event.

best_facts.fact: Nagaland's Hornbill Festival, which already feels traditional, was created by the state government in 2000.

side_dish.title: Fireflies that hold a festival
side_dish.body_md:
In the Great Smoky Mountains of the United States, for about two weeks between late May and June, thousands of male fireflies of the species *Photinus carolinus* do something that looks like a festival. They flash together, a burst of five to eight quick blinks in near-perfect unison, then the whole forest goes dark for several seconds, then they flash again.

For decades scientists doubted the local stories. A naturalist named **Lynn Faust**, who had watched them since childhood at her family cabin at Elkmont, brought them to researchers' attention in the 1990s. Today the US National Park Service runs a **lottery** for viewing passes, because so many people want to see it.

How do the fireflies coordinate without a leader? Each male adjusts its own rhythm slightly towards the flashes it sees. Small nudges, repeated across thousands of insects, lock the whole group into one beat. Mathematicians such as **Steven Strogatz** have shown the same logic governs heart pacemaker cells, applause that falls into rhythm, and footsteps on a wobbling bridge. In the mangroves of Malaysia and Thailand, *Pteroptyx* fireflies do it on whole trees.

Now think back to the fire-walk and Thaipusam. Humans at a festival are doing a version of the same thing: clapping, chanting, dancing and even heartbeats nudging towards each other until a crowd becomes one rhythm. Synchrony is one of nature's oldest ways of turning many into one.

offline_task.title: Catch a crowd falling into rhythm
offline_task.body_md:
Next time you are in any group (a puja, a wedding sangeet, a cricket match, a concert, a school assembly, even a long applause), watch for the moment it **synchronises**.

1. Notice when clapping or chanting stops being random and locks into one beat. How long did it take? Who started it?
2. Join in deliberately for one minute. Then stop and just watch for one minute. Notice any difference in how close you feel to the people around you.
3. Ask one older relative which festival they miss most from childhood, and what exactly they miss: the food, the people, the noise, the ritual, or the break from work. Write down their answer in one sentence.

Bring that sentence back tomorrow. You will probably find it maps onto one of today's six theories.
